"Instead of discarding winter garden prunings through burning or shredding, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This sustainable approach offers multiple benefits: it serves as an excellent windbreak, provides a safe haven for local wildlife, and can effectively delineate different sections of your garden plot. To construct one, simply drive stakes or repurposed fence posts into the ground, creating two parallel rows approximately 50cm apart. Then, begin slotting your pruned material between these posts, placing the larger branches at the base for stability. As you continue to add more plant matter, the hedge will naturally compact and settle over time, becoming more robust.

If your Christmas gifts left something to be desired, a perfect pick-me-up could be pre-ordering "The Book Of Seeds" by Paul Smith, former head of Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. This lavish guide, due for release in February from Ivy Press (£30), showcases 600 of the planet's most unusual and breathtaking seed species. Readers can expect to discover fascinating examples, ranging from seeds with striking, hair-like features reminiscent of Donald Trump's coiffure to the incredibly minute, pinhead-sized seeds of orchids.

For gardeners looking to add beauty and interest during the colder months, winter-flowering clematis is an exceptional choice. Given a sunny and protected location, these plants will reward you with an abundance of blooms between December and February. Cultivars such as Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ (growing to 3m x 1.5m) and C. cirrhosa var. balearica (reaching 2.5m x 1.5m) boast creamy, fragrant flowers accented with maroon markings. Alternatively, C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ offers pure white blossoms and can achieve a more substantial size of 5m x 2m, providing a stunning display."
